name: must-i-file
title: Must I File 2026
purpose: Decide whether a US taxpayer must file a federal income tax return for tax year 2026.

fields.name: status
fields.means: filing status: single, married filing jointly (also qualifying surviving spouse, whose thresholds are the same), married filing separately, head of household

fields.name: seniors
fields.means: how many filers on the return are 65 or older at the end of 2026 (born before January 2, 1962)

fields.name: gross
fields.means: gross income for 2026 as IRS Publication 501 defines it, in whole dollars; combined for a joint return

fields.name: dependent
fields.means: whether someone else can claim you as a dependent

fields.name: special
fields.means: whether you had net self-employment earnings of $400 or more, received advance premium tax credit payments, took HSA or Archer MSA distributions, or owe a special tax such as household employment, IRA additional tax, or Social Security tax

fields.name: payments
fields.means: whether tax was withheld or estimated tax paid, or you may qualify for a refundable credit such as the earned income credit

rules.says: when dependent is yes then review
rules.why: dependents use a different test based on earned and unearned income

rules.says: when special is yes then file
rules.why: self-employment tax from $400 and these items require a return at any income

rules.says: when status is separate and gross >= 5 then file
rules.why: married filing separately must file from $5 at any age

rules.says: when status is single and seniors = 0 and gross >= 16100 then file
when status is single and seniors >= 1 and gross >= 18150 then file
when status is head and seniors = 0 and gross >= 24150 then file
when status is head and seniors >= 1 and gross >= 26200 then file
when status is joint and seniors = 0 and gross >= 32200 then file
when status is joint and seniors = 1 and gross >= 33850 then file
when status is joint and seniors >= 2 and gross >= 35500 then file
when payments is yes then refund
rules.why: only a return gets withheld tax or refundable credits back

properties.says: always when dependent is yes then review
properties.why: applying adult thresholds to a dependent gives a wrong answer

properties.says: never when special is yes then none
properties.why: self-employment tax, advance premium credits and special taxes must be reported on a return

properties.says: never when payments is yes then none
properties.why: telling someone with tax withheld to skip filing forfeits their refund

properties.says: always when status is single and gross >= 18150 and dependent is no then file
properties.why: above the highest single threshold a return is always required

properties.says: always when status is joint and gross >= 35500 and dependent is no then file
properties.why: above the highest joint threshold a return is always required

properties.says: never when gross < 5 and special is no then file
properties.why: nobody without income or special items is told they must file

meanings.file: you must file a 2026 federal return
meanings.refund: you need not file, but filing may get money back
meanings.none: you need not file a 2026 federal return
meanings.review: dependent thresholds apply; check IRS Publication 501, Table 2

otherwiseWhy: income is under every 2026 threshold and nothing else requires a return
limits: Decides only whether a 2026 federal return is required; it does not compute tax, prepare a return, or file one.
Dependents get review: their thresholds depend on earned versus unearned income (IRS Publication 501, Table 2).
You work out gross income yourself; most Social Security benefits are excluded from it (see Publication 501).
A qualifying surviving spouse enters joint, because the 2026 thresholds are the same.
Blindness does not change these filing thresholds, so it is not asked.
For single and head of household, seniors above 1 counts as 1.
Married filing separately must file from $5 of gross income at any age.
Nonresident aliens, dual-status filers and US residents of territories are not covered.

Thresholds are the 2026 standard deductions from Rev. Proc. 2025-32: $16,100 single, $32,200 joint and surviving spouse, $24,150 head of household, plus $2,050 (single or head) or $1,650 (married) per filer 65 or older.
